entries.7101ab25f92ec39148ee143e21f477fbf564a97e: <div sID="gen3401" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Deut.3" sID="Deut.3"/> <div eID="gen3401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3402" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3403" type="x-p"/> Moses, in this chapter, relates, I. The conquest of Og, king of Bashan, and the seizing of his country, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.1-Deut.3.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. The distribution of these new conquests to the two tribes and a half, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.12-Deut.3.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. Under certain provisos and limitations, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.18-Deut.3.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. III. The encouragement given to Joshua to carry on the war which was so gloriously begun, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.21-Deut.3.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. IV. Moses's request to go over into Canaan (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.23-Deut.3.25">ver. 23-25</reference>), with the denial of that request, but the grant of an equivalent, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.26-Deut.3.29">ver. 26</reference>, &c.
entries.a93fe533e51077ca4e9d11e6ffe82698a1e48c78: <div eID="gen3403" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3402" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sihon and Og Subdued. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3404" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then we turned, and went up the way to Bashan: and Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Fear him not: for I will deliver him, and all his people, and his land, into thy hand; and thou shalt do unto him as thou didst unto Sihon king of the Amorites, which dwelt at Heshbon. <hi type="super">3</hi> So the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God delivered into our hands Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people: and we smote him until none was left to him remaining. <hi type="super">4</hi> And we took all his cities at that time, there was not a city which we took not from them, threescore cities, all the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. <hi type="super">5</hi> All these cities <hi type="italic">were</hi> fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many. <hi type="super">6</hi> And we utterly destroyed them, as we did unto Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying the men, women, and children, of every city. <hi type="super">7</hi> But all the cattle, and the spoil of the cities, we took for a prey to ourselves. <hi type="super">8</hi> And we took at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites the land that <hi type="italic">was</hi> on this side Jordan, from the river of Arnon unto mount Hermon; <hi type="super">9</hi> (<hi type="italic">Which</hi> Hermon the Sidonians call Sirion; and the Amorites call it Shenir;) <hi type="super">10</hi> All the cities of the plain, and all Gilead, and all Bashan, unto Salchah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. <hi type="super">11</hi> For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead <hi type="italic">was</hi> a bedstead of iron; <hi type="italic">is</hi> it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? nine cubits <hi type="italic">was</hi> the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man. <div eID="gen3404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3405" type="x-p"/> We have here another brave country delivered into the hand of Israel, that of Bashan; the conquest of Sihon is often mentioned together with that of Og, to the praise of God, the rather because in these Israel's triumphs began, <reference osisRef="Ps.135.11">Ps. cxxxv. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.136.19-Ps.136.20">cxxxvi. 19, 20</reference>. See, <div eID="gen3405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3406" type="x-p"/> I. How they got the mastery of Og, a very formidable prince, 1. Very strong, for he was of the remnant of the giants (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.11">v. 11</reference>); his personal strength was extraordinary, a monument of which was preserved by the Ammonites in his bedstead, which was shown as a rarity in their chief city. You might guess at his weight by the materials of his bedstead; it was iron, as if a bedstead of wood were too weak for him to trust to: and you might guess at his stature by the dimensions of it; it was nine cubits long and four cubits broad, which, supposing a cubit to be but half a yard (and some learned men have made it appear to be somewhat more), was four yards and a half long, and two yards broad; and if we allow his bedstead to be two cubits longer than himself, and that is as much as we need allow, he was three yards and a half high, double the stature of an ordinary man, and every way proportionable, yet they smote him, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.3">v. 3</reference>. Note, when God pleads his people's cause he can deal with giants as with grasshoppers. No man's might can secure him against the Almighty. The army of Og was very powerful, for he had the command of sixty fortified cities, besides the unwalled towns, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.5">v. 5</reference>. Yet all this was nothing before God's Israel, when they came with commission to destroy him. 2. He was very bold and daring: He <hi type="italic">came out against Israel to battle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.3.1">v. 1</reference>. It was wonderful that he did not take warning by the ruin of Sihon, and send to desire conditions of peace; but he trusted to his own strength, and so was hardened to his destruction. Note, Those that are not awakened by the judgments of God upon others, but persist in their defiance of heaven, are ripening apace for the like judgments upon themselves, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.8">Jer. iii. 8</reference>. God bade Moses not fear him, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.2">v. 2</reference>. If Moses himself was so strong in faith as not to need the caution, yet it is probable that the people needed it, and for them these fresh assurances are designed; "<hi type="italic">I will deliver him into thy hand;</hi> not only deliver thee out of his hand, that he shall not be thy ruin, but deliver him <hi type="italic">into thy hand,</hi> that thou shalt be his ruin, and make him pay dearly for his attempt." He adds, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt do to him as thou didst to Sihon,</hi> intimating that they ought to be encouraged by their former victory to trust in God for another victory, for he is God, and changeth not. <div eID="gen3406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3407" type="x-p"/> II. How they got possession of Bashan, a very desirable country. They took all the cities (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">v. 4</reference>), and all the spoil of them, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.7">v. 7</reference>. They made them all their own, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">v. 10</reference>. So that now they had in their hands all that fruitful country which lay east of Jordan, from <hi type="italic">the river Arnon unto Hermon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.3.8">v. 8</reference>. Their conquering and possessing these countries was intended, not only for the encouragement of Israel in the wars of Canaan, but for the satisfaction of Moses before his death. Since he must not live to see the completing of their victory and settlement, God thus gives him a specimen of it. Thus the Spirit is given to those that believe as the <hi type="italic">earnest of their inheritance,</hi> until the redemption of the purchased possession.
entries.f64fb10472de0c77b8b2d8632f72689904681185: <div eID="gen3407" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Allotment of the Conquered Lands. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3408" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And this land, <hi type="italic">which</hi> we possessed at that time, from Aroer, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the river Arnon, and half mount Gilead, and the cities thereof, gave I unto the Reubenites and to the Gadites. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, <hi type="italic">being</hi> the kingdom of Og, gave I unto the half tribe of Manasseh; all the region of Argob, with all Bashan, which was called the land of giants. <hi type="super">14</hi> Jair the son of Manasseh took all the country of Argob unto the coasts of Geshuri and Maachathi; and called them after his own name, Bashan-havoth-jair, unto this day. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I gave Gilead unto Machir. <hi type="super">16</hi> And unto the Reubenites and unto the Gadites I gave from Gilead even unto the river Arnon half the valley, and the border even unto the river Jabbok, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> the border of the children of Ammon; <hi type="super">17</hi> The plain also, and Jordan, and the coast <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> from Chinnereth even unto the sea of the plain, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the salt sea, under Ashdoth-pisgah eastward. <hi type="super">18</hi> And I commanded you at that time, saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath given you this land to possess it: ye shall pass over armed before your brethren the children of Israel, all <hi type="italic">that are</hi> meet for the war. <hi type="super">19</hi> But your wives, and your little ones, and your cattle, (<hi type="italic">for</hi> I know that ye have much cattle,) shall abide in your cities which I have given you; <hi type="super">20</hi> Until the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have given rest unto your brethren, as well as unto you, and <hi type="italic">until</hi> they also possess the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath given them beyond Jordan: and <hi type="italic">then</hi> shall ye return every man unto his possession, which I have given you. <div eID="gen3408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3409" type="x-p"/> Having shown how this country which they were now in was conquered, in these verses he shows how it was settled upon the Reubenites, Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, which we had the story of before, <reference osisRef="Num.32.1-Num.32.42">Num. xxxii.</reference> Here is the rehearsal. 1. Moses specifies the particular parts of the country that were allotted to each tribe, especially the distribution of the lot to the half tribe of Manasseh, the subdividing of which tribe is observable. Joseph was divided into Ephraim and Manasseh; Manasseh was divided into one half on the one side Jordan and the other half on the other side: that on the east side Jordan was again divided into two great families, which had their several allotments: Jair, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">v. 14</reference>, Machir, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.15">v. 15</reference>. And perhaps Jacob's prediction of the smallness of that tribe was now accomplished in these divisions and subdivisions. Observe that Bashan is here called <hi type="italic">the land of the giants,</hi> because it had been in their possession, but Og was the last of them. These giants, it seems, had lost their country, and were rooted out of it sooner than any of their neighbours; for those who, presuming upon their strength and stature, had their hand against every man, had every man's hand against them, and went down slain to the pit, though they were the terror of the mighty in the land of the living. 2. He repeats the condition of the grant which they had already agreed to, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.18-Deut.3.20">v. 18-20</reference>. That they should send a strong detachment over Jordan to lead the van in the conquest of Canaan, who should not return to their families, at least not to settle (though for a time they might retire thither into winter quarters, at the end of a campaign), till they had seen their brethren in as full possession of their respective allotments as they themselves were now in of theirs. They must hereby be taught not to <hi type="italic">look at their own things only, but at the things of others,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.4">Phil. ii. 4</reference>. It ill becomes an Israelite to be selfish, and to prefer any private interest before the public welfare. When we are rest we should desire to see our brethren at rest too, and should be ready to do what we can towards it; for we are not born for ourselves, but are members one of another. A good man cannot rejoice much in the comforts of his family unless withal he sees <hi type="italic">peace upon Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.128.6">Ps. cxxviii. 6</reference>.
entries.51339a51824efea74c1397909eb5023ea11ba752: <div eID="gen3409" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joshua Named as Moses's Successor. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3410" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And I commanded Joshua at that time, saying, Thine eyes have seen all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God hath done unto these two kings: so shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> do unto all the kingdoms whither thou passest. <hi type="super">22</hi> Ye shall not fear them: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God he shall fight for you. <hi type="super">23</hi> And I besought the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> at that time, saying, <hi type="super">24</hi> O Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , thou hast begun to show thy servant thy greatness, and thy mighty hand: for what God <hi type="italic">is there</hi> in heaven or in earth, that can do according to thy works, and according to thy might? <hi type="super">25</hi> I pray thee, let me go over, and see the good land that <hi type="italic">is</hi> beyond Jordan, that goodly mountain, and Lebanon. <hi type="super">26</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was wroth with me for your sakes, and would not hear me: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter. 27 Get thee up into the top of Pisgah, and lift up thine eyes westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold <hi type="italic">it</hi> with thine eyes: for thou shalt not go over this Jordan. <hi type="super">28</hi> But charge Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him: for he shall go over before this people, and he shall cause them to inherit the land which thou shalt see. <hi type="super">29</hi> So we abode in the valley over against Beth-peor. <div eID="gen3410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3411" type="x-p"/> Here is I. The encouragement which Moses gave to Joshua, who was to succeed him in the government, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.21-Deut.3.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. He commanded him not to fear. Thus those that are aged and experienced in the service of God should do all they can to strengthen the hands of those that are young, and setting out in religion. Two things he would have him consider for his encouragement:—1. What God has done. Joshua had seen what a total defeat God had given by the forces of Israel to these two kings, and thence he might easily infer, <hi type="italic">so shall the Lord do to all the rest of the kingdoms</hi> upon which we are to make war. He must not only infer thence that thus the Lord can do with them all, for his arm is not shortened, but thus he will do, for his purpose is not changed; he that has begun will finish; <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect.</hi> Joshua had seen it with his own eyes. And the more we have seen of the instances of divine wisdom, power, and goodness, the more inexcusable we are if we <hi type="italic">fear what flesh can do unto us.</hi> 2. What God had promised. The <hi type="italic">Lord your God he shall fight for you;</hi> and that cause cannot but be victorious which the Lord of hosts fights for. <hi type="italic">If God be for us, who can be against us</hi> so as to prevail? We reproach our leader if we follow him trembling. <div eID="gen3411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3412" type="x-p"/> II. The prayer which Moses made for himself, and the answer which God gave to that prayer. <div eID="gen3412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3413" type="x-p"/> 1. His prayer was that, if it were God's will, he might go before Israel over Jordan into Canaan. At that time, when he had been encouraging Joshua to fight Israel's battles, taking it for granted that he must be their leader, he was touched with an earnest desire to go over himself, which expresses itself not in any passionate and impatient complaints, or reflections upon the sentence he was under, but in humble prayers to God for a gracious reversing of it. <hi type="italic">I besought the Lord.</hi> Note, We should never allow any desires in our hearts which we cannot in faith offer up to God by prayer; and what desires are innocent, let them be presented to God. We have not because we ask not. Observe, <div eID="gen3413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3414" type="x-p"/> (1.) What he pleads here. Two things:— [1.] The great experience which he had had of God's goodness to him in what he had done for Israel: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast begun to show thy servant thy greatness.</hi> Lord, perfect what thou hast begun. Thou hast given me to see thy glory in the conquest of these two kings, and the sight has affected me with wonder and thankfulness. O let me see more of the outgoings of my God, my King! This great work, no doubt, will be carried on and completed; let me have the satisfaction of seeing it." Note, the more we see of God's glory in his works the more we shall desire to see. <hi type="italic">The works of the Lord are great,</hi> and therefore are sought out more and more <hi type="italic">of all those that have pleasure therein.</hi> [2.] The good impressions that had been made upon his heart by what he had seen: For <hi type="italic">what God is there in heaven or earth that can do according to thy works?</hi> The more we are affected with what we have seen of God, of his wisdom, power, and goodness, the better we are prepared for further discoveries. Those shall see the works of God that admire him in them. Moses had thus expressed himself concerning God and his works long before (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exod. xv. 11</reference>), and he still continues of the same mind, that there are no works worthy to be compared with God's works, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.8">Ps. lxxxvi. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen3414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3415" type="x-p"/> (2.) What he begs: <hi type="italic">I pray thee let me go over,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.3.25">v. 25</reference>. God had said he should not go over; yet he prays that he might, not knowing but that the threatening was conditional, for it was not ratified with an oath, as that concerning the people was, that they should not enter. Thus Hezekiah prayed for his own life, and David for the life of his child, after both had been expressly threatened; and the former prevailed, though the latter did not. Moses remembered the time when he had by prayer prevailed with God to recede from the declarations which he had made of his wrath against Israel, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.14">Exod. xxxii. 14</reference>. And why might he not hope in like manner to prevail for himself? <hi type="italic">Let me go over and see the good land.</hi> Not, "Let me go over and be a prince and a ruler there;" he seeks not his own honour, is content to resign the government to Joshua; but, "Let me go to be a spectator of thy kindness to Israel, to see what I believe concerning the goodness of the land of promise." How pathetically does he speak of Canaan, that <hi type="italic">good land,</hi> that <hi type="italic">goodly mountain!</hi> Note, Those may hope to obtain and enjoy God's favours that know how to value them. What he means by <hi type="italic">that goodly mountain</hi> we may learn from <reference osisRef="Ps.78.54">Ps. lxxviii. 54</reference>, where it is said of God's Israel that <hi type="italic">he brought them to the border of his sanctuary, even to this mountain which his right hand had purchased,</hi> where it is plainly to be understood of the whole land of Canaan, yet with an eye to the sanctuary, the glory of it. <div eID="gen3415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3416" type="x-p"/> 2. God's answer to this prayer had in it a mixture of mercy and judgment, that he might sing unto God of both. <div eID="gen3416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3417" type="x-p"/> (1.) There was judgment in the denial of his request, and that in something of anger too: <hi type="italic">The Lord was wroth with me for your sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.3.26">v. 26</reference>. God not only sees sin in his people, but is much displeased with it; and even those that are delivered from the wrath to come may yet lie under the tokens of God's wrath in this world, and may be denied some particular favour which their hearts are much set upon. God is a gracious, tender, loving Father; but he is angry with his children when they do amiss, and denies them many a thing that they desire and are ready to cry for. But how was he wroth with Moses <hi type="italic">for the sake of Israel?</hi> Either, [1.] For that sin which they provoked him to; see <reference osisRef="Ps.106.32-Ps.106.33">Ps. cvi. 32, 33</reference>. Or, [2.] The removal of Moses at that time, when he could so ill be spared, was a rebuke to all Israel, and a punishment of their sin. Or, [3.] It was for their sakes, that it might be a warning to them to take heed of offending God by passionate and unbelieving speeches at any time, after the similitude of his transgression; for, if <hi type="italic">this were done to such a green tree, what should be done to the dry?</hi> He acknowledges that God would not hear him. God had often heard him for Israel, yet he would not hear him for himself. It was the prerogative of Christ, the great Intercessor, to be heard always; yet of him his enemies said, <hi type="italic">He saved others, himself he could not save,</hi> which the Jews would not have upbraided him with had they considered that Moses, their great prophet, prevailed for others, but for himself he could not prevail. Though Moses, being one of the wrestling seed of Jacob, did not seek in vain, yet he had not the thing itself which he sought for. God may accept our prayers, and yet not grant us the very thing we pray for. <div eID="gen3417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3418" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is mercy mixed with this wrath in several things:—[1.] God quieted the spirit of Moses under the decree that had gone forth by that word (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.26">v. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let it suffice thee.</hi> With this word, no doubt, a divine power went to reconcile Moses to the will of God, and to bring him to acquiesce in it. If God does not by his providence give us what we desire, yet, if by his grace he makes us content without it, it comes much to one. "<hi type="italic">Let it suffice thee</hi> to have God for thy father, and heaven for thy portion, though thou hast not every thing thou wouldest have in this world. Be satisfied with this, <hi type="italic">God is all-sufficient.</hi>" [2.] He put an honour upon his prayer in directing him not to insist upon this request: <hi type="italic">Speak no more to me of this matter.</hi> It intimates that what God does not think fit to grant we should not think fit to ask, and that God takes such a pleasure in the prayer of the upright that it is no pleasure to him, no, not in any particular instance, to give a denial to it. [3.] He promised him a sight of Canaan <hi type="italic">from the top of Pisgah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.3.27">v. 27</reference>. Though he should not have the possession of it, he should have the prospect of it; not to tantalize him, but such a sight of it as would yield him true satisfaction, and would enable him to form a very clear and pleasing idea of that promised land. Probably Moses had not only his sight preserved for other purposes, but greatly enlarged for this purpose; for, if he had not had such a sight of it as others could not have from the same place, it would have been no particular favour to Moses, nor the matter of a promise. Even great believers, in this present state, see heaven but at a distance. [4.] He provided him a successor, one who should support the honour of Moses and carry on and complete that glorious work which the heart of Moses was so much upon, the bringing of Israel to Canaan, and settling them there (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">Charge Joshua and encourage him</hi> in this work. Those to whom God gives a charge, he will be sure to give encouragement to. And it is a comfort to the church's friends (when they are dying and going off) to see God's work likely to be carried on by other hands, when they are silent in the dust.  <chapter eID="Deut.3"/> <div eID="gen3418" type="x-p"/>

entries.ae6eb69ea6e8d7939a894919516e53834f057110: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1669"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.3.1-Deut.3.20">De 3:1-20</reference>. Conquest of Og, King of Bashan.</title> <div sID="gen2234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1669"/><hi type="bold">1. we turned, and went up the way to Bashan--</hi>Bashan ("fruitful" or "flat"), now El-Bottein, lay situated to the north of Gilead and extended as far as Hermon. It was a rugged mountainous country, valuable however for its rich and luxuriant pastures.<div eID="gen2234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Og the king of Bashan came out against us--</hi>Without provocation, he rushed to attack the Israelites, either disliking the presence of such dangerous neighbors, or burning to avenge the overthrow of his friends and allies. <div eID="gen2235" type="x-p"/>
entries.745d56c1bbef7b1f16e9931b7728666e8e78b0c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1670"/><div sID="gen2236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1670"/><hi type="bold">2. The Lord said unto me, Fear him not: for I will deliver him, and all his people, and his land, into thy hand--</hi>Og's gigantic appearance and the formidable array of forces he will bring to the field, need not discourage you; for, belonging to a doomed race, he is destined to share the fate of Sihon [Nu 21:25]. <div eID="gen2236" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbf4957ae1cd69e744cbaa12d6d0702066b240d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1671"/><div sID="gen2237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1671"/><hi type="bold">3-8. Argob was the capital of a district in Bashan of the same name, which, together with other fifty-nine cities in the same province, were conspicuous for their lofty and fortified walls. It was a war of extermination. Houses and cities were razed to the ground; all classes of people were put to the sword; and nothing was saved but the cattle, of which an immense amount fell as spoil into the hands of the conquerors. Thus, the two Amorite kings and the entire population of their dominions were extirpated. The whole country east of the Jordan--</hi>first upland downs from the torrent of the Arnon on the south to that of the Jabbok on the north; next the high mountain tract of Gilead and Bashan from the deep ravine of Jabbok--became the possession of the Israelites. <div eID="gen2237" type="x-p"/>
entries.c91992ca103ace13d17fb4c8a886b3c5bce1e6d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1672"/><div sID="gen2238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1672"/><hi type="bold">9. Hermon--</hi>now Jebel-Es-Sheick--the majestic hill on which the long and elevated range of Anti-Lebanon terminates. Its summit and the ridges on its sides are almost constantly covered with snow. It is not so much one high mountain as a whole cluster of mountain peaks, the highest in Palestine. According to the survey taken by the English Government Engineers in 1840, they were about 9376 feet above the sea. Being a mountain chain, it is no wonder that it should have received different names at different points from the different tribes which lay along the base--all of them designating extraordinary height: Hermon, the lofty peak; "Sirion," or in an abbreviated form "Sion" (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.48">De 4:48</reference>), the upraised, glittering; "Shenir," the glittering breastplate of ice. <div eID="gen2238" type="x-p"/>
entries.1910b64325bcc31e99aecc93d63e977708273d59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1673"/><div sID="gen2239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1673"/><hi type="bold">11. only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants--</hi>literally, "of Rephaim." He was not the last giant, but the only living remnant in the trans-jordanic country (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.14">Jos 15:14</reference>), of a certain gigantic race, supposed to be the most ancient inhabitants of Palestine.<div eID="gen2239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron--</hi>Although beds in the East are with the common people nothing more than a simple mattress, bedsteads are not unknown. They are in use among the great, who prefer them of iron or other metals, not only for strength and durability, but for the prevention of the troublesome insects which in warm climates commonly infest wood. Taking the cubit at half a yard, the bedstead of Og would measure thirteen and a half feet, so that as beds are usually a little larger than the persons who occupy them, the stature of the Amorite king may be estimated at about eleven or twelve feet; or he might have caused his bed to be made much larger than was necessary, as Alexander the Great did for each of his foot soldiers, to impress the Indians with an idea of the extraordinary strength and stature of his men [Le Clerc]. But how did Og's bedstead come to be in Rabbath, of the children of Ammon? In answer to this question, it has been said, that Og had, on the eve of engagement, conveyed it to Rabbath for safety. Or it may be that Moses, after capturing it, may have sold it to the Ammonites, who had kept it as an antiquarian curiosity till their capital was sacked in the time of David. This is a most unlikely supposition, and besides renders it necessary to consider the latter clause of this verse as an interpolation inserted long after the time of Moses. To avoid this, some eminent critics take the Hebrew word rendered "bedstead" to mean "coffin." They think that the king of Bashan having been wounded in battle, fled to Rabbath, where he died and was buried; hence the dimensions of his "coffin" are given [Dathe, Roos]. <div eID="gen2240" type="x-p"/>
entries.95cb32cdbe636da678d7488471388813f90c2370: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1674"/><div sID="gen2241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1674"/><hi type="bold">12-13. this land, which we possessed at that time, from Aroer ... gave I unto the Reubenites and to the Gadites--</hi>The whole territory occupied by Sihon was parcelled out among the pastoral tribes of Reuben and Gad. It extended from the north bank of the Arnon to the south half of mount Gilead--a small mountain ridge, now called Djelaad, about six or seven miles south of the Jabbok, and eight miles in length. The northern portion of Gilead and the rich pasture lands of Bashan--a large province, consisting, with the exception of a few bleak and rocky spots, of strong and fertile soil--was assigned to the half-tribe of Manasseh. <div eID="gen2241" type="x-p"/>
entries.15dfd8d69cc16bc612863b723e6140e8e4d2e717: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1675"/><div sID="gen2242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1675"/><hi type="bold">14. Jair the son of Manasseh took all the country of Argob--</hi>The original inhabitants of the province north of Bashan, comprising sixty cities (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">De 3:4</reference>), not having been extirpated along with Og, this people were afterwards brought into subjection by the energy of Jair. This chief, of the tribe of Manasseh, in accordance with the pastoral habits of his people, called these newly acquired towns by a name which signifies "Jair's Bedouin Villages of Tents."<div eID="gen2242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto this day--</hi>This remark must evidently have been introduced by Ezra, or some of the pious men who arranged and collected the books of Moses. <div eID="gen2243" type="x-p"/>
entries.290eb91d113ed6f143326fc059f15097c1757bf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1676"/><div sID="gen2244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1676"/><hi type="bold">15. I gave Gilead unto Machir--</hi>It was only the half of Gilead (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.12">De 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">13</reference>) which was given to the descendants of Machir, who was now dead. <div eID="gen2244" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff1daecfec8e67e7b6dc24a0595523bd35b1970b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1677"/><div sID="gen2245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1677"/><hi type="bold">16. from Gilead--</hi>that is, not the mountainous region, but the town Ramoth-gilead,<div eID="gen2245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even unto the river Arnon half the valley--</hi>The word "valley" signifies a wady, either filled with water or dry, as the Arnon is in summer, and thus the proper rendering of the passage will be--"even to the half or middle of the river Arnon" (compare <reference osisRef="Josh.12.2">Jos 12:2</reference>). This prudent arrangement of the boundaries was evidently made to prevent all disputes between the adjacent tribes about the exclusive right to the water. <div eID="gen2246" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb037af0be328755df828e1bb75feb7607cc343c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1678"/><div sID="gen2247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1678"/><hi type="bold">25. I pray thee, let me go over, and see the good land that is beyond Jordan, that goodly mountain, and Lebanon--</hi>The natural and very earnest wish of Moses to be allowed to cross the Jordan was founded on the idea that the divine threatening might be conditional and revertible. "That goodly mountain" is supposed by Jewish writers to have pointed to the hill on which the temple was to be built (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.5">De 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Ex 15:2</reference>). But biblical scholars now, generally, render the words--"that goodly mountain, even Lebanon," and consider it to be mentioned as typifying the beauty of Palestine, of which hills and mountains were so prominent a feature. <div eID="gen2247" type="x-p"/>
entries.012353f8fccc4cfdf5df33bd7682fd51a8f5f210: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1679"/><div sID="gen2248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1679"/><hi type="bold">26. speak no more unto me of this matter--</hi>that is, My decree is unalterable. <chapter eID="Deut.3"/>

entries.06eb238dce93804f9c2c88801381a6805e5cf253: <div eID="gen6452" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6453" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6454" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6454" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6453" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6455" type="x-p"/> The war with Og, king of Bashan, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.1">Deu 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.2">Deu 3:2</reference>. He is defeated, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.3">Deu 3:3</reference>. Sixty fortified cities with many unwalled towns taken, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.4">Deu 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.5">Deu 3:5</reference>. The utter destruction of the people, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.6">Deu 3:6</reference>. The spoils, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.7">Deu 3:7</reference>; and extent of the land taken, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.8-Deu.3.10">Deu 3:8-10</reference>. Account of Og's iron bedstead, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.11">Deu 3:11</reference>. The land given to the Reubenites, Gadites, and half tribe of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.12">Deu 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>. Jair takes the country of Argob, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>. Gilead is given unto Machir, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.15">Deu 3:15</reference>. And the rest of the land possessed by the Reubenites and Gadites, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.16">Deu 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.17">Deu 3:17</reference>. The directions given to those tribes, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.18-Deu.3.20">Deu 3:18-20</reference>. The counsel given to Joshua, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.21">Deu 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.22">Deu 3:22</reference>. Moses's prayer to God for permission to go into the promised land, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.23-Deu.3.25">Deu 3:23-25</reference>; and God's refusal, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.26">Deu 3:26</reference>. He is commanded to go up to Mount Pisgah to see it, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.27">Deu 3:27</reference>; and to encourage Joshua, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.28">Deu 3:28</reference>. They continue in the valley opposite to Beth-peor, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.29">Deu 3:29</reference>.
entries.67313ad3473407dc989f86e45893fa2a072ea9eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen6455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6456" type="x-p"/> All the region of Argob - כל חבל ארגב col chebel Argob, all the cable or cord of Argob; this expression, which is used in various other parts of Scripture, (see, in the original, <reference osisRef="Amo.7.17">Amo 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.5">Mic 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.32.9">Deu 32:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference>), shows that anciently land was measured by lines or cords of a certain length, in a similar way to that by the chain among us, and the schoenus or cord among the Egyptians. Some think that it was the region of Argob that was afterwards called the region of Trachonites.
entries.39d537fc21ca2728915dcceb87804ce779dbaa32: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen6456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6457" type="x-p"/> Hermon the Sidonians call - Shenir - I suppose this verse to have been a marginal remark, which afterwards got incorporated with the text, or an addition by Joshua or Ezra.
entries.2ebe7960318ce54751b5d46bace77f068cf12f7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen6457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6458" type="x-p"/> Og king of Bashan remained - Og was the last king of the Amorites; his kingdom appears to have taken its name from the hill of Bashan; the country has been since called Batanaea. <div eID="gen6458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6459" type="x-p"/> Remnant of giants - Of the Rephaim. See on <reference osisRef="Deu.2.10">Deu 2:10</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Deu.2.11">Deu 2:11</reference> (note). <div eID="gen6459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6460" type="x-p"/> His bedstead was - of iron - Iron was probably used partly for its strength and durability, and partly to prevent noxious vermin from harbouring in it. <div eID="gen6460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6461" type="x-p"/> Is it not in Rabbath, of the children of Ammon? - The bedstead was probably taken in some battle between the Ammonites and Amorites, in which the former had gained the victory. The bedstead was carried a trophy and placed in Rabbath, which appears, from <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26">2Sam 12:26</reference>, to have been the royal city of the children of Ammon. <div eID="gen6461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6462" type="x-p"/> Nine cubits was the length - four cubits the breadth - Allowing the bedstead to have been one cubit longer than Og, which is certainly sufficient, and allowing the cubit to be about eighteen inches long, for this is perhaps the average of the cubit of a man, then Og was twelve feet high. This may be deemed extraordinary, and perhaps almost incredible, and therefore many commentators have, according to their fancy, lengthened the bedstead and shortened the man, making the former one-third longer than the person who lay on it, that they might reduce Og to six cubits; but even in this way they make him at least nine feet high. <div eID="gen6462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6463" type="x-p"/> On this subject the rabbins have trifled most sinfully. I shall give one specimen. In the Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel on <reference osisRef="Num.21.33-Num.21.35">Num 21:33-35</reference>, it is said that "Og having observed that the camp of the Israelites extended six miles, he went and tore up a mountain six miles in its base, and put it on his head, and carried it towards the camp, that he might throw it on the Israelites and destroy them; but the word of the Lord prepared a worm, which bored a hole in the mountain over his head, so that it fell down upon his shoulders: at the same time his teeth growing out in all directions, stuck into the mountain, so that he could not cast it off his head. Moses, (who was himself ten cubits high), seeing Og thus entangled, took an axe ten cubits long, and having leaped ten cubits in height, struck Og on the ankle bone, so that he fell and was slain." <div eID="gen6463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6464" type="x-p"/> From this account the distance from the sole of Og's foot to his ankle was thirty cubits in length! I give this as a very slight specimen of rabbinical comment. I could quote places in the Talmud in which Og is stated to be several miles high! This relation about Og I suppose to be also an historical note added by a subsequent hand.
entries.56f5ed73bfbe01b6ed32e34a0ed13464b2bdfaf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen6464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6465" type="x-p"/> Bashan-havoth-jair - Bashan of the cities of Jair; see <reference osisRef="Num.32.41">Num 32:41</reference>.
entries.dac08a87bc110701b115be7afec5384752f0c699: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen6465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6466" type="x-p"/> From Chinnereth - See on <reference osisRef="Num.34.11">Num 34:11</reference> (note).
entries.967e15efd650da5415db39d71af34787ee858d7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen6466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6467" type="x-p"/> The prayer of Moses recorded in these two verses, and his own reflections on it, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.26">Deu 3:26</reference>, are very affecting. He had suffered much both in body and mind in bringing the people to the borders of the promised land; and it was natural enough for him to wish to see them established in it, and to enjoy a portion of that inheritance himself, which he knew was a type of the heavenly country. But notwithstanding his very earnest prayer, and God's especial favor towards him, he was not permitted to go over Jordan! He had grieved the Spirit of God, and he passed a sentence against him of exclusion from the promised land. Yet he permitted him to see it, and gave him the fullest assurances that the people whom he had brought out of Egypt should possess it. Thus God may choose to deprive those of earthly possessions to whom he is nevertheless determined to give a heavenly inheritance.
entries.f39f39b57e2300ee94f226ab8f7e82fbe5f7995c: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen6467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6468" type="x-p"/> Let it suffice thee - רב לך rab lach, there is an abundance to thee - thou hast had honor enough already, and may well dispense with going over Jordan. He surely has no reason to complain who is taken from earthly felicity to heavenly glory. In this act God showed to Moses both his goodness and severity.
entries.69482f8abd6adbe13bcb8b3f9eed1a4f742bd60c: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen6468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6469" type="x-p"/> But charge Joshua, etc. - Give him authority in the sight of the people, let them see that he has the same commission which I gave to thee. Encourage him; for he will meet with many difficulties in the work to which he is called. And strengthen him - show him my unfailing promises, and exhort him to put his trust in me alone; for he shall go over before this people, and shall cause them to inherit the land; of this let him rest perfectly assured.
entries.1debbab7d7cd2a81d55485d17b0177cc36f23afc: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen6469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6470" type="x-p"/> Beth-peor - This was a city in the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites; and as בית beth signifies a house, the place probably had its name from a temple of the god Peor, who was worshipped there. Peor was nearly the same among the Moabites that Priapus was among the Romans - the obscene god of an obscene people. This we have already seen. <div eID="gen6470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6471" type="x-p"/> It is very likely that what God speaks here, both concerning Moses and Joshua, was designed to be typical of the procedure of his justice and grace in the salvation of man. <div eID="gen6471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6472" type="x-p"/> 1. The land of Canaan was a type of the kingdom of heaven. <div eID="gen6472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6473" type="x-p"/> 2. The law, which shows the holiness of God and the exceeding sinfulness of sin, could not bring the people to the possession of that kingdom. <div eID="gen6473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6474" type="x-p"/> 3. Moses may probably be considered here as the emblem of that law by which is the knowledge of sin, but not redemption from it <div eID="gen6474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6475" type="x-p"/> 4. Joshua, the same as Jesus, the name signifying a Savior, is appointed to bring the people into the rest which God had provided for them; thus it is by Jesus Christ alone that the soul is saved - fitted for and brought into the possession of the heavenly inheritance, (see <reference osisRef="Joh.1.17">Joh 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.16">Gal 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">Gal 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Gal 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.24">Gal 3:24</reference>); for he is the end of the law - the great scope and design of the law, for righteousness - for justification, to them that believe; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">Rom 10:4</reference>. Such a use as this every pious reader may make of the circumstances recorded here, without the danger of pushing analogy or metaphor beyond their reasonable limits.  <chapter eID="Deut.3"/> <div eID="gen6475" type="x-p"/>

entries.f7319232fac33b10e93c8e889815b5b1043d1936: <reference osisRef="Deut.3.1-Deut.3.9">Deu 3:1-9</reference> <div eID="gen2157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2158" type="x-p"/> The Help of God in the Conquest of the Kingdom of Og of Bashan. - Deu 3:1. After the defeat of king Sihon and the conquest of his land, the Israelites were able to advance to the Jordan. But as the powerful Amoritish king Og still held the northern half of Gilead and all Bashan, they proceeded northwards at once and took the road to Bashan, that they might also defeat this king, whom the Lord had likewise given into their hand, and conquer his country (cf. Num 21:33-34). They smote him at Edrei, the modern <hi type="italic">Draà</hi>, without leaving him even a remnant; and took all his towns, i.e., as is here more fully stated in Deu 3:4., “sixty <hi type="italic">towns, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan</hi>.” These three definitions refer to one and the same country. The whole region of Argob included the sixty towns which formed the kingdom of Og in Bashan, i.e., all the towns of the land of Bashan, viz., (according to <reference osisRef="Deut.3.5">Deu 3:5</reference>) all the fortified towns, besides the unfortified and open country towns of Bashan. חבל, the chain for measuring, then the land or country measured with the chain. The name “<hi type="italic">region of Argob</hi>,” which is given to the country of Bashan here, and in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">Deu 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>, and also in 1Ki 4:13, is probably derived from רגוב, stone-heaps, related to רגב, a clump or clod of earth (<reference osisRef="Job.21.33">Job 21:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.38">Job 38:38</reference>). The Targumists have rendered it correctly טרכונא (<hi type="italic">Trachona</hi>), from τραθών, a rough, uneven, stony district, so called from the basaltic hills of Hauran; just as the plain to the east of Jebel Hauran, which resembles Hauran itself, is sometimes called <hi type="italic">Tellul</hi>, from its tells or hills (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, Syr. p. 173).<note placement="foot">The derivation is a much more improbable one, “from the town of <hi type="italic">Argob</hi>, πρὸς Γέρασαν πόλιν Ἀραβίας, according to the<hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>., fifteen Roman miles to the west of <hi type="italic">Gerasa</hi>, which is called Ῥαγαβᾶ by <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Ant. xiii. 15, 5).”</note> <div eID="gen2158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2159" type="x-p"/> This district has also received the name of <hi type="italic">Bashan</hi>, from the character of its soil; for בּשׁן signifies a soft and level soil. From the name given to it by the Arabic translators, the Greek name Βαταναία, <hi type="italic">Batanaea</hi>, and possibly also the modern name of the country on the north-eastern slope of Hauran at the back of Mount Hauran, viz., <hi type="italic">Bethenije</hi>, are derived. <div eID="gen2159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2160" type="x-p"/> The name <hi type="italic">Argob</hi> probably originated in the north-eastern part of the country of Bashan, viz., the modern <hi type="italic">Leja</hi>, with its stony soil covered with heaps of large blocks of stone (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, p. 196), or rather in the extensive volcanic region to the east of Hauran, which was first of all brought to distinct notice in <hi type="italic">Wetzstein's</hi> travels, and of which he says that the “southern portion, bearing the name <hi type="italic">Harra</hi>, is thickly covered with loose volcanic stones, with a few conical hills among them, that have been evidently caused by eruptions” (<hi type="italic">Wetzstein</hi>, p. 6). The central point of the whole is <hi type="italic">Safa</hi>, “a mountain nearly seven hours’ journey in length and about the same in breadth,” in which “the black mass streaming from the craters piled itself up wave upon wave, so that the centre attained to the height of a mountain, without acquiring the smoothness of form observable in mountains generally,” - “the black flood of lava being full of innumerable streams of stony waves, often of a bright red colour, bridged over with thin arches, which rolled down the slopes out of the craters and across the high plateau” (<hi type="italic">Wetzstein</hi>, pp. 6 and 7). At a later period this name was transferred to the whole of the district of Hauran (= Bashan), because not only is the Jebel Hauran entirely of volcanic formation, but the plain consists throughout of a reddish brown soil produced by the action of the weather upon volcanic stones, and even “the <hi type="italic">Leja</hi> plain has been poured out from the craters of the Hauran mountains” (<hi type="italic">Wetzstein</hi>, p. 23). Through this volcanic character of the soil, Hauran differs essentially from Balka, Jebel <hi type="italic">Ajlun</hi>, and the plain of <hi type="italic">Jaulan</hi>, which is situated between the Sea of Galilee and the upper Jordan on the one side, and the plain of Hauran on the other, and reaches up to the southern slope of the Hermon. In these districts the limestone and chalk formations prevail, which present the same contrast to the basaltic formation of the Hauran as white does to black (cf. <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> pp. 75ff.). - The land of the limestone and chalk formation abounds in caves, which are not altogether wanting indeed in Hauran (as <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi> supposes), though they are only found in eastern and south-eastern Hauran, where most of the volcanic elevations have been perforated by troglodytes (see Wetzstein, pp. 92 and 44ff.). But the true land of caves on the east of the Jordan is northern Gilead, viz., <hi type="italic">Erbed</hi> and <hi type="italic">Suêt</hi> (<hi type="italic">Wetzst</hi>. p. 92). Here the troglodyte dwellings predominate, whereas in Hauran you find for the most part towns and villages with houses of one or more stories built above the surface of the ground, although even on the eastern slope of the Hauran mountains there are hamlets to be seen, in which the style of building forms a transition from actual caves to dwellings built upon the ground. An excavation is first of all made in the rocky plateau, of the breadth and depth of a room, and this is afterwards arched over with a solid stone roof. The dwellings made in this manner have all the appearance of cellars or tunnels. This style of building, such as <hi type="italic">Wetzstein</hi> found in <hi type="italic">Hibbike</hi> for example, belongs to the most remote antiquity. In some cases, hamlets of this kind were even surrounded by a wall. Those villages of Hauran which are built above the surface of the ground, attract the eye and stimulate the imagination, when seen from a distance, in various ways. “In the first place, the black colour of the building materials present the greatest contrast to the green around them, and to the transparent atmosphere also. In the second place, the height of the walls and the compactness of the houses, which always form a connected whole, are very imposing. In the third place, they are surmounted by strong towers. And in the fourth place, they are in such a good state of preservation, that you involuntarily yield to the delusion that they must of necessity be inhabited, and expect to see people going out and in” (<hi type="italic">Wetzstein</hi>, p. 49). The larger towns are surrounded by walls; but the smaller ones as a rule have none: “the backs of the houses might serve as walls.” The material of which the houses are built is a grey dolerite, impregnated with glittering particles of olivine. “The stones are rarely cemented, but the fine and for the most part large squares lie one upon another as if they were fused together.” “Most of the doors of the houses which lead into the streets or open fields are so low, that it is impossible to enter them without stooping; but the large buildings and the ends of the streets have lofty gateways, which are always tastefully constructed, and often decorated with sculptures and Greek inscriptions.” The “larger gates have either simple or (what are most common) double doors. They consist of a slab of dolerite. There are certainly no doors of any other kind.” These stone doors turn upon pegs, deeply inserted into the threshold and lintel. “Even a man can only shut and open doors of this kind, by pressing with the back or feet against the wall, and pushing the door with both hands” (<hi type="italic">Wetzstein</hi>, pp. 50ff.; compare with this the testimony of <hi type="italic">Buckingham, Burckhardt,</hi> <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, and others, in <hi type="italic">v. Raumer's</hi> Palestine, pp. 78ff.). <div eID="gen2160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2161" type="x-p"/> Now, even if the existing ruins of Hauran date for the most part from a later period, and are probably of a Nabataean origin belonging to the times of Trajan and the Antonines, yet considering the stability of the East, and the peculiar nature of the soil of Hauran, they give a tolerably correct idea of the sixty towns of the kingdom of Og of Bashan, all of which were fortified with high walls, gates, and bars, or, as it is stated in 1Ki 4:13, “with walls and brazen bars.”<note placement="foot">It is also by no means impossible, that many of the oldest dwellings in the ruined towers of Hauran date from a time anterior to the conquest of the land by the Israelites. “Simple, built of heavy blocks of basalt roughly hewn, and as hard as iron, with very thick walls, very strong stone gates and doors, many of which were about eighteen inches thick, and were formerly fastened with immense bolts, and of which traces still remain; such houses as these may have been the work of the old giant tribe of Rephaim, whose king, Og, was defeated by the Israelites 3000 years ago” (<hi type="italic">C. v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> p. 80, after <hi type="italic">Porter's</hi> Five Years in Damascus).</note> <div eID="gen2161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2162" type="x-p"/> The brazen bars were no doubt, like the gates themselves, of basalt or dolerite, which might easily be mistaken for brass. Besides the sixty fortified towns, the Israelites took a very large number of הפּרזי ערי, “<hi type="italic">towns of the inhabitants of the flat country</hi>,” i.e., unfortified open hamlets and villages in Bashan, and put them under the ban, like the towns of king Sihon (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.6">Deu 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.7">Deu 3:7</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.2.34-Deut.2.35">Deu 2:34-35</reference>). The infinitive, החרם, is to be construed as a gerund (cf. <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §131, 2; <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §280, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). The expression, “kingdom of Og <hi type="italic">in</hi> Bashan,” implies that the kingdom of Og was not limited to the land of Bashan, but included the northern half of Gilead as well. In <reference osisRef="Deut.3.8-Deut.3.11">Deu 3:8-11</reference>, Moses takes a retrospective view of the whole of the land that had been taken on the other side of the Jordan; first of all (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.9">Deu 3:9</reference>) in its whole extent from the Arnon to Hermon, then (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference>) in its separate parts, to bring out in all its grandeur what the Lord had done for Israel. The notices of the different names of Hermon (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.9">Deu 3:9</reference>), and of the bed of king Og (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.11">Deu 3:11</reference>), are also subservient to this end. <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi> is the southernmost spur of Antilibanus, the present <hi type="italic">Jebel es Sheikh</hi>, or Jebel <hi type="italic">et Telj</hi>. The Hebrew name is not connected with חרם, <hi type="italic">anathema</hi>, as Hengstenberg supposes (Diss. pp. 197-8); nor was it first given by the Israelites to this mountain, which formed part of the northern boundary of the land which they had taken; but it is to be traced to an Arabic word signifying <hi type="italic">prominens montis vertex</hi>, and was a name which had long been current at that time, for which the Israelites used the Hebrew name שׂיאן (<hi type="italic">Sion</hi> = נשׂיאן, the high, eminent: <reference osisRef="Deut.4.48">Deu 4:48</reference>), though this name did not supplant the traditional name of <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi>. The Sidonians called it <hi type="italic">Siron</hi>, a modified form of שׁריון   (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.5">1Sa 17:5</reference>), or נשׂיון (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.4">Jer 46:4</reference>), a “coat of mail;” the Amorites called it <hi type="italic">Senir</hi>, probably a word with the same meaning. In <reference osisRef="Ps.29.6">Psa 29:6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Sirion</hi> is used poetically for <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi>; and Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">Eze 27:4</reference>) uses <hi type="italic">Senir</hi>, in a mournful dirge over Tyre, as synonymous with <hi type="italic">Lebanon</hi>; whilst <hi type="italic">Senir</hi> is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.23">1Ch 5:23</reference>, and Shenir in Sol 4:8, in connection with Hermon, as a part of Antilibanus, as it might very naturally happen that the Amoritish name continued attached to one or other of the peaks of the mountain, just as we find that even Arabian geographers, such as <hi type="italic">Abulfeda</hi> and <hi type="italic">Maraszid</hi>, call that portion of Antilibanus which stretches from Baalbek to Emesa (Homs, Heliopolis) by the name of <hi type="italic">Sanir</hi>.
entries.dc05612cf90e99a7955eb4f933cae6ca8428ac05: <reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference> <div eID="gen2162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2163" type="x-p"/> The different portions of the conquered land were the following: המּישׁר, <hi type="italic">the plain</hi>, i.e., the Amoritish table-land, stretching from the Arnon to Heshbon, and in a north-easterly direction nearly as far as Rabbath-Ammon, with the towns of <hi type="italic">Heshbon, Bezer, Medeba, Jahza,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Dibon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.43">Deu 4:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.9">Jos 13:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16-Josh.13.17">Jos 13:16-17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.21">Jos 13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.20.8">Jos 20:8</reference>; Jer 48:21.), which originally belonged to the Moabites, and is therefore called “the field of Moab” in Num 21:20. “<hi type="italic">The whole of Gilead</hi>,” i.e., the mountainous region on the southern and northern sides of the Jabbok, which was divided into two halves by this river. The southern half, which reached to Heshbon, belonged to the kingdom of Sihon (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.2">Jos 12:2</reference>), and was assigned by Moses to the Reubenites and Gadites (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.12">Deu 3:12</reference>); whilst the northern half, which is called “the rest of Gilead” in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>, the modern Jebel <hi type="italic">Ajlun</hi>, extending as far as the land of Bashan (Hauran and Jaulan), belonged to the kingdom of Og (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>), and was assigned to the Manassite family of Machir (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.15">Deu 3:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Josh.13.31">Jos 13:31</reference>; cf. <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> pp. 229, 230). “<hi type="italic">And all Bashan unto Salcah and Edrei</hi>.” All Bashan included not only the country of Hauran (the plan and mountain), but unquestionably also the district of <hi type="italic">Jedur</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jaulan</hi>, to the west of the sea of Galilee and the upper Jordan, or the ancient <hi type="italic">Gaulonitis</hi> (Jos.<hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> xviii. 4, 6, etc.), as the kingdom of Og extended to the coasts of Geshuri and Maachathi (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>). Og had not conquered the whole of the land of Hauran, however, but only the greater part of it. His territory extended eastwards to <hi type="italic">Salcah</hi>, i.e., the present <hi type="italic">Szalchat</hi> or <hi type="italic">Szarchad</hi>, about six hours to the east of <hi type="italic">Bozrah</hi>, south of Jebel Hauran, a town with 800 houses, and a castle upon a basaltic rock, but uninhabited (cf. <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> p. 255); and northwards to <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi>, i.e., the northern <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi> (see at Num 21:33), a considerable ruin on the northwest of <hi type="italic">Bozrah</hi>, three or four English miles in extent, in the old buildings of which there are 200 families living at present (Turks, Druses, and Christians). By the Arabian geographers (<hi type="italic">Abulfeda, Ibn Batuta</hi>) it is called Sora, by modern travellers Adra or <hi type="italic">Edra</hi> (<hi type="italic">v. Richter</hi>), or <hi type="italic">Oezraa</hi> (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>), or <hi type="italic">Ezra</hi> (<hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>), and <hi type="italic">Edhra</hi> (Robinson, App. 155). Consequently nearly the whole of Jebel Hauran, and the northern portion of the plain, viz., the <hi type="italic">Leja</hi>, were outside the kingdom of Og and the land of Bashan, of which the Israelites took possession, although <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi> reckons Ezra as part of the Leja.
entries.72aa96969c0ced7dc9466e4b26127d8e9abfea04: <reference osisRef="Deut.3.11">Deu 3:11</reference> <div eID="gen2163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2164" type="x-p"/> Even in Abraham’s time, the giant tribe of <hi type="italic">Rephaim</hi> was living in Bashan (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Gen 14:5</reference>). But out of the remnant of these, king Og, whom the Israelites defeated and slew, was the only one left. For the purpose of recalling the greatness of the grace of God that had been manifested in that victory, and not merely to establish the credibility of the statements concerning the size of Og (“just as things belonging to an age that has long passed away are shown to be credible by their remains,” <hi type="italic">Spinoza</hi>, etc.), Moses points to the iron bed of this king, which was still in Rabbath-Ammon, and was nine cubits long and four broad, “after the cubit of a man,” i.e., the ordinary cubit in common use (see the analogous expression, “a man’s pen,” <reference osisRef="Isa.8.1">Isa 8:1</reference>). הלה, for הלא, synonymous with הנּה. There is nothing to amaze is in the size of the bed or bedstead given here. The ordinary Hebrew cubit was only a foot and a half, probably only eighteen Dresden inches (see my <hi type="italic">Archäologie</hi>, ii. p. 126, Anm. 4). Now a bed is always larger than the man who sleeps in it. But in this case <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> fancies that Og “intentionally exceeded the necessary size, in order that posterity might be led to draw more magnificent conclusions from the size of the bed, as to the stature of the man who was accustomed to sleep in it.” He also refers to the analogous case of Alexander the Great, of whom <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> (xvii. 95) affirms, that whenever he was obliged to halt on his march to India, he made colossal arrangements of all kinds, causing, among other things, two couches to be prepared in the tents for every foot-soldier, each five cubits long, and two stalls for every horseman, twice as large as the ordinary size, “to represent a camp of heroes, and leave striking memorials behind for the inhabitants of the land, of gigantic men and their supernatural strength.” With a similar intention Og may also have left behind him a gigantic bed as a memorial of his superhuman greatness, on the occasion of some expedition of his against the Ammonites; and this bed may have been preserved in their capital as a proof of the greatness of their foe.<note placement="foot">“It will often be found, that very tall people are disposed to make themselves appear even taller than they actually are” (Hengstenberg, Diss. ii. p. 201). Moreover, there are still giants who are eight feet high and upwards. “According to the <hi type="italic">N. Preuss. Zeit.</hi> of 1857, there came a man to Berlin 8 feet 4 inches high, and possibly still growing, as he was only twenty years old; and he was said to have a great-uncle who was nine inches taller” (<hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>).</note> <div eID="gen2164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2165" type="x-p"/> Moses might then refer to this gigantic bed of Og, which was known to the Israelites; and there is no reason for resorting to the improbable conjecture, that the Ammonites had taken possession of a bed of king Og upon some expedition against the Amorites, and had carried it off as a trophy to their capital.<note placement="foot">There is still less probability in the conjecture of <hi type="italic">J. D. Michaelis, Vater, Winer, </hi>and others, that Og’s iron bed was a sarcophagus of basalt, such as are still frequently met with in those regions, as much as 9 feet long and 3 1/2 feet broad, or even as much as 12 feet long and 6 feet in breadth and height (vid., <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, pp. 220, 246; Robinson, iii. p. 385; <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, i. pp. 355, 360); and the still further assumption, that the corpse of the fallen king was taken to Rabbah, and there interred in a royal way, is altogether improbable.</note> <div eID="gen2165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2166" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Rabbath</hi> of the sons of Ammon,” or briefly <hi type="italic">Rabbah</hi>, i.e., the great (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.25">Jos 13:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">2Sa 11:1</reference>), was the capital of the Ammonites, afterwards called <hi type="italic">Philadelphia</hi>, probably from Ptolemaeus Philadelphus; by <hi type="italic">Polybius</hi>, Ῥαββατάμανα; by <hi type="italic">Abulfeda</hi>, <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi>, which is the name still given to the uninhabited ruins on the <hi type="italic">Nahr Ammân</hi>, i.e., the upper Jabbok (see <hi type="italic">Burckhardt</hi>, pp. 612ff. and <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> p. 268).
entries.1b8484d6d06aec2c7fd75dad25c7bab90f2ecf46: <reference osisRef="Deut.3.12-Deut.3.13">Deu 3:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen2166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2167" type="x-p"/> Review of the Distribution of the Conquered Land. - The land which the Israelites had taken belonging to these two kingdoms was given by Moses to the two tribes and a half for their possession, viz., the southern portion from Aroer in the Arnon valley (see at Num 32:34), and half Gilead (as far as the Jabbok: see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.10">Deu 3:10</reference>) with its towns, which are enumerated in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.15-Josh.13.20">Jos 13:15-20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.13.24-Josh.13.28">Jos 13:24-28</reference>, to the Reubenites and Gadites; and the northern half of Gilead, with the whole of Bashan (i.e., all the region of Argob: see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">Deu 3:4</reference>, and Num 32:33), to the half-tribe of Manasseh. לכל־הבּשׁן, “<hi type="italic">as for all Bashan</hi>,” is in apposition to “<hi type="italic">all the region of Argob</hi>,” and the ל simply serves to connect it; for “all the region of Argob” was not merely one portion of Bashan, but was identical with “all Bashan,” so far as it belonged to the kingdom of Og (see at v. 4). All this region passed for a land of giants. הקּרא, to be called, i.e., to be, and to be recognised as being.
entries.78c2563b00bd657c67d83bd8ca43832ad28e56e2: <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference> <div eID="gen2167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2168" type="x-p"/> The region of Argob, or the country of Bashan, was given to <hi type="italic">Jair</hi> (see Num 32:41), as far as the territory of the Geshurites and Maachathites (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.11">Jos 13:11</reference>). “<hi type="italic">Unto</hi>,” as far as, is to be understood as inclusive. This is evident from the statement in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.13">Jos 13:13</reference> : “The <hi type="italic">children of Israel expelled not the Geshurites nor the Maachathites; but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day</hi>.” Consequently Moses allotted the territory of these two tribes to the Manassites, because it formed part of the kingdom of Og. “<hi type="italic">Geshuri and Maachathi</hi>” are the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi> and <hi type="italic">Maachah</hi>, two provinces which formed small independent kingdoms even in David’s time (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.3">2Sa 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.37">2Sa 13:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference>). <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi> bordered on Aram. The Geshurites and Aramaeans afterwards took from the Israelites the <hi type="italic">Jair</hi>-towns and <hi type="italic">Kenath</hi>, with their daughter towns (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.23">1Ch 2:23</reference>). In David’s time <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi> had a king <hi type="italic">Thalmai</hi>, whose daughter David married. This daughter was the mother of Absalom; and it was in Geshur that Absalom lived for a time in exile (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.3">2Sa 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.37">2Sa 13:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.23">2Sa 14:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.8">2Sa 15:8</reference>). The exact situation of <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi> has not yet been determined. It was certainly somewhere near Hermon, on the eastern side of the upper Jordan, and by a <hi type="italic">bridge</hi> over the Jordan, as <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi> signifies bridge in all the Semitic dialects. <hi type="italic">Maachah</hi>, which is referred to in <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6">1Ch 19:6</reference> as a kingdom under the name of <hi type="italic">Aram-Maachah</hi> (Eng. V. Syria-Maachah), is probably to be sought for to the north-east of <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi>. According to the <hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>. (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> Μαχαθί), it was in the neighbourhood of the Hermon. “<hi type="italic">And he called them</hi> (the towns of the region of Argob) <hi type="italic">after his own name; Bashan</hi> (sc., he called) <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair unto this day</hi>” (cf. Num 32:41). The word חוּת (<hi type="italic">Havvoth</hi>), which only occurs in connection with the <hi type="italic">Jair</hi>-towns, does not mean towns or camps of a particular kind, viz., tent villages, as some suppose, but is the plural of חוּה, life (<hi type="italic">Leben</hi>, a common German termination, e.g., <hi type="italic">Eisleben</hi>), for which afterwards the word חיּה was used (comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">2Sa 23:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>). It applies to any kind of dwelling-place, being used in the passages just mentioned to denote even a warlike encampment. The <hi type="italic">Jair's-lives</hi> (<hi type="italic">Jairsleben</hi>) were not a particular class of towns, therefore, in the district of Argob, but Jair gave this collective name to all the sixty fortified towns, as is perfectly evident from the verse before us when compared with <reference osisRef="Deut.3.5">Deu 3:5</reference> and Num 32:41, and expressly confirmed by <reference osisRef="Josh.13.30">Jos 13:30</reference> and 1Ki 4:13, where the sixty fortified towns of the district of Argob are called <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair</hi>. - The statement in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.22-1Chr.2.23">1Ch 2:22-23</reference>, that “<hi type="italic">Jair had twenty-three towns in Gilead</hi> (which is used here as in <reference osisRef="Deut.34.1">Deu 34:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.22.9">Jos 22:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.15">Jos 13:15</reference>; Jdg 5:17; Jdg 20:1, to denote the whole of Palestine to the east of the Jordan), <hi type="italic">and Geshur and Aram took the Havvoth Jair from them</hi>, (and) <hi type="italic">Kenath and its daughters, sixty towns</hi> (sc., in all),” is by no means at variance with this, but, on the contrary, in the most perfect harmony with it. For it is evident from this passage, that the twenty-three Havvoth Jair, with Kenath and its daughters, formed sixty towns altogether. The distinction between the twenty-three <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair</hi> and the other thirty-seven towns, viz., <hi type="italic">Kenath</hi> and its daughters, is to be explained from the simple fact that, according to Num 32:42, <hi type="italic">Nobah</hi>, no doubt a family of sons of Machir related to Jair, conquered Kenath and its daughters, and called the conquered towns by his name, namely, when they had been allotted to him by Moses. Consequently Bashan, or the region of Argob, with its sixty fortified towns, was divided between two of the leading families of Machir the Manassite, viz., the families of <hi type="italic">Jair</hi> and <hi type="italic">Nobah</hi>, each family receiving the districts which it had conquered, together with their towns; namely, the family of <hi type="italic">Nobah</hi>, Kenath and its daughter towns, or the eastern portion of Bashan; and the family of <hi type="italic">Jair</hi>, twenty-three towns in the west, which are called <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.23">1Ch 2:23</reference>, in harmony with Num 32:41, where Jair is said to have given this name to the towns which were conquered by him. In the address before us, however, in which Moses had no intention to enter into historical details, all the (sixty) towns of the whole district of Argob, or the whole of Bashan, are comprehended under the name of <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair</hi>, probably because <hi type="italic">Nobah</hi> was a subordinate branch of the family of <hi type="italic">Jair</hi>, and the towns conquered by him were under the supremacy of Jair. The expression “unto this day” certainly does not point to a later period than the Mosaic age. This definition of time is simply a relative one. It does not necessarily presuppose a very long duration, and here it merely serves to bring out the marvellous change which was due to the divine grace, viz., that the sixty fortified towns of the giant king Og of Bashan had now become Jair’s lives.<note placement="foot">The conquest of these towns, in fact, does not seem to have been of long duration, and the possession of them by the Israelites was a very disputed one (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.22-1Chr.2.23">1Ch 2:22-23</reference>). In the time of the judges we find thirty in the possession of the judge <hi type="italic">Jair</hi> (Jdg 10:4), which caused the old name <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair</hi> to be revived.</note>
entries.dd50b56faf730784bef773a1f5586406f7ba5ca3: <reference osisRef="Deut.3.15-Deut.3.20">Deu 3:15-20</reference> <div eID="gen2168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2169" type="x-p"/> Machir received Gilead (see Num 32:40). - In <reference osisRef="Deut.3.16">Deu 3:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.3.17">Deu 3:17</reference> the possession of the tribes of Reuben and Gad is described more fully according to its boundaries.
